newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dollar learns to live with lower rates.
newsitem.headline: Australian dollar learns to live with lower rates.

text.p: The Australian dollar put in a resilient performance Thursday, suggesting the market was learning to live with the prospect of lower rates.
A fifth rate cut seemed a certainty after wages data proved surprisingly subdued, so confirming the impressive price outlook portrayed in Wednesday's historically low inflation figures.

"The policy equation is one of low actual inflation, low prospective inflation and high unemployment," said Bruce Freeland, chief economist at Commonwealth Bank. "There would appear to be only one solution to this, another rate cut."
By 4.30 pm (0630 GMT) the currency was putting a brave face on the prospect at US$0.7348/53 having crept up from a US$0.7327 low, to be not far off Wednesday's late US$0.7373/78.

The numerate in the market have seen the easing coming for some weeks and the dollar had already fallen more than four cents in anticipation, begging the question of whether a 50 basis point cut to 5.00 percent was now fully discounted.
Many thought it was.
"One hundred and fifty percent," was the answer from Citibank forex head Steve Shuster when asked how much of the cut was priced in. "This is the most anticipated easing ever."
Indeed, so utter was the expectation, and so frustrating the waiting, he felt the A$ would rally in relief once it was over.
"The Aussie's holding up well given almost every negative you can think of has been thrown at it," he said.

"The world's short after selling dollars for four months and it would only take one of the big hedge or momentum funds to start taking some back for the Aussie to really rock -- and, ironically, a rate cut could be the trigger."
He saw scope to reach US$0.7450 on short covering while chart watchers felt a break of the US$0.7475 barrier would suggest the downtrend from 80 cents had bottomed here at 73.
Conversely, a breach of US$0.7305 -- the trough from January 1996 -- would indicate the trend had further to run and risk a return to the 1995 low, and Fibonacci point, of US$0.7070/7100.
Analysts said the Reserve Bank might move as early as Friday morning -- which would also serve a public relations exercise in explicitly rewarding the wage restraint evident in today's data.

The figures showed average weekly ordinary time earnings rose a modest 0.5 percent in the May quarter dragging annual growth down to 3.7 percent from 4.3 in Q1, the lowest rise in almost three years. Forecasts had favoured gains of 0.8 percent and 4.1 percent respectively.

The annual rise was well below the 4.5 percent danger line which the RBA regarded as a threat to inflation and would come as a huge relief to the bank which had long been frustrated by the stubborness of wage growth.

The weak wages data argued for a cut in a second way in that it implied the earnings, salaries and supplements contribution to GDP growth would be low in the June quarter -- if pay rises were lower then people did not have so much to spend.
The futures market certainly saw the figures as a green light and chased the September 90-day bank bill contract seven basis points higher to 94.96, implying a rate of 5.04 percent.

The comparable Eurodollar future was at 94.275 reflecting the risk the Federal Reserve may hike the 5.50 percent funds sometime down the track, so the A$ already effectively yielded around 75 basis points less than the US$.

This was a new, and not entirely welcome, experience for a market used to thinking of the A$ as a high yielder and it was taking time for investors to accept Australian fundamentals were good enough that it should not require a risk premium.
The process was proceeding apace in the bond market where the yield spread on local and U.S. 10-year bonds had shrunk from over 200 basis points a couple of years ago to just 29 today.
And the 10-year bond future briefly touched a record high of 93.640 before finishing five basis points up at 93.570.
The growing offshore confidence in Australia this narrowing reflected should be supportive of the dollar in the longer term and perhaps limit the shockwave should the RBA finally ease.
On the crosses the dollar was steady at 85.10/20 yen from 84.95/05 Wednesday and extended a rally on a weak mark to 1.3433/47 from 1.3408/20.
It was still a shade down in trade weighted terms at 57.1 from 57.1 late Wednesday.
-- Sydney newsroom 61-2 9373 1800
